From these photos, your operation looks much more organized than it did earlier. There are several improvements that stand out immediately.

### What is working well

- **The banner is excellent.** It is readable from a long distance, the colors have high contrast, and "FRIED CATFISH" dominates exactly as it should. It catches the eye.

- **The serving station is much cleaner.** The hotel pans with lids keep the fish covered and give the setup a more professional appearance than having food exposed.

- **The two scales are a smart addition.** Having one for bagging portions and one for customer-facing weighing supports the "1½ pounds for $20" concept and helps reduce disputes.

- **Consumables are consolidated.** Bread, containers, bags, and utensils are all grouped together in bins instead of scattered around the table.

- **The condiment tray looks organized.** Customers can immediately see hot sauce and tartar packets.

- **Your trash can is lined and positioned conveniently.** That's something inspectors often notice.

- **The fryer area is separated from the serving area.** Keeping the hot oil behind the serving table is good practice.

---

### Things I would improve next

#### 1. Hide the gray totes

The gray storage totes are practical, but they still look like storage containers rather than part of a food business.

If you eventually replace them with black bus tubs or stainless hotel pans, the whole stand will look more like a commercial kitchen.

---

#### 2. Raise the banner

The banner nearly touches the tops of your head when you're working.

Raising it another 8–12 inches would:
- make the stand feel more open,
- improve visibility,
- prevent it from visually "closing off" the booth.

---

#### 3. Add one menu sign

The biggest thing missing is a price.

Someone walking by should know within two seconds:

> **1½ Pounds Fresh Fried Catfish**
>
> **$20**

Without asking.

---

#### 4. Cover the serving table

The black tabletop works, but a fitted black tablecloth would hide the legs and storage underneath and make the booth look significantly more polished.

---

#### 5. Shield the propane tanks

The propane setup looks functional, but it's the first thing my eye is drawn to after the banner.

If practical and allowed by your local regulations, a simple nonflammable screen or placing the tote slightly farther behind the booth could keep the tanks from dominating the view while still leaving them accessible.

---

### One operational suggestion

The stainless hotel pan holding cooked fish is a nice improvement.

If you're cooking to order, I'd avoid accumulating too many pieces in that pan. Keeping only the current order—or perhaps one sample piece—maintains the perception that every customer is getting fish that just came out of the fryer.

---

## Overall impression

Compared with your earlier setup, I'd rate this as:

- **Visibility:** 9.5/10
- **Organization:** 9/10
- **Professional appearance:** 8.5/10
- **Customer confidence:** 9/10

The biggest remaining improvement isn't equipment—it's making the offer unmistakable. A customer walking by should instantly read:

> **FRIED CATFISH**  
> **1½ POUNDS • $20**

Once that information is visible from a distance, you'll likely reduce hesitation from people who are interested but don't want to stop just to ask the price.

## My recommendation

**Buy that exact box.**

It lets you use **one screw type for the entire project**, which keeps things simple and avoids carrying multiple boxes of fasteners. The only remaining hardware you'll need beyond these screws is:

- 1" #10 fender washers (for the tarps)

Exactly. That's the tradeoff I should have mentioned.

If you simply cross two round EMT tubes, one **must** sit on top of the other.

For 1/2" EMT, the outside diameter is about **0.706 inches**, so the centerlines of the two tubes are separated by about that amount.

```
Side View

──────────────  Horizontal EMT

       ↑
   ~0.706"

       │
       │
       │
    Vertical EMT
```

For your application, that's actually **not a problem**. The tarp doesn't care if the horizontal member is offset by 0.7 inches.

The only consequence is that the joint is **eccentric** (the centerlines don't intersect), so tightening a single bolt can allow the horizontal tube to roll slightly.

That's why I was recommending two bolts or another anti-rotation feature.

### I actually think there's an even simpler solution.

Rather than trying to make a true tee, let the **horizontal EMT simply terminate against the side of the vertical EMT.**

```
Top View

Horizontal EMT
─────────────●

             │
             │
             │
          Vertical EMT
```

Drill two holes through the end of the horizontal conduit and bolt it to the vertical conduit.

Now the horizontal member is acting like a cantilever beam supported by the vertical post. For the small loads from a tarp, that's perfectly reasonable.

Alternatively, if you want the horizontal to continue past the vertical, you can still overlap them, but I'd use **two bolts** spaced a few inches apart to resist twisting.

So yes—one pipe will always sit above the other unless you use a manufactured tee fitting or notch one of the pipes. For a lightweight tarp frame, the offset is small enough that it shouldn't materially affect the performance of the structure.

EMT                 EMT

### Materials

- 2 × 3/4" EMT conduit, 10 ft (uprights)
- 1 × 3/4" EMT conduit, 5 ft (crossbar, cut from a 10 ft stick)
- 2 × 3/4" EMT 90° elbows (compression or setscrew type)
- 2 × umbrella stand bases, sandbags, or concrete blocks

No diagonal bracing.

No screws into wood.

No carpentry.

---

## Option 2 – EMT with Floor Feet

Instead of weights:

```
Top View

─────────┼─────────
      24" EMT
```

Materials

- 2 × EMT Tee fittings
- 4 × EMT end caps

The tees make "T" feet.

This is still easy to assemble.

## Option 3 – One Upright + Existing Wall (Simplest Overall)

Since one edge of the tarp is against an existing wall, you may only need one support.

```
Existing wall

│─────────────── EMT ───────────────●

                                   │
                                   │
                                   │
                              Single EMT upright
```

Materials

- 2 × EMT conduit
- 1 × 90° elbow
- 1 × weighted base

Half as many parts.

---

# The Fittings

This is the confusing part because Home Depot stocks several kinds.

I would **avoid standard electrical EMT couplings and elbows** intended for wiring. They are made to join conduit in permanent electrical installations, not to build frames.

Instead, look in the chain-link fence or canopy hardware area—or online—for **EMT structural fittings**. Common brands include:

- Maker Pipe
- Hollaender Speed-Rail
- SteelTek

These are specifically designed to turn EMT conduit into furniture, frames, greenhouses, and workstations.

For your project, the only fittings you really need are:

| Qty | Fitting | Purpose |
|----:|---------|---------|
| 2 | 90° corner fittings | Connect uprights to top crossbar |
| 2 | Tee fittings *(if using feet)* | Attach floor feet to uprights |
| 4 | End caps | Finish the feet |

---

## If you want the absolute easiest construction

I would actually skip building feet from EMT altogether.

Buy:

- 3 × 3/4" EMT conduit
- 2 × structural 90° corner fittings (Maker Pipe or SteelTek style)
- 2 × umbrella stand bases (or heavy planter bases)

Then simply insert each upright into a weighted base. This eliminates all the tee fittings, end caps, measuring, and extra cuts. You end up with a rigid, portable frame that assembles in minutes and can later be expanded if you decide to enclose more of the workstation.

If you're already heading to Home Depot, I can also narrow this down to **specific aisle items** (including Maker Pipe, SteelTek, or Everbilt hardware if your local store stocks them) and estimate the total cost.

I agree with that approach. This is a utility enclosure, not finished carpentry. You can always upgrade it later with grommets if the tarp starts to wear.

For **today**, I'd buy exactly this:

## Screws

**#10 × 1-1/4" Exterior Construction Screws**

Why:

- Long enough to bite securely into the stud.
- Large enough to clamp the tarp well.
- Easy to drive.

**#10 Stainless Steel Fender Washers**

```text
Screw

↓

1" Fender Washer

↓

Tarp

↓

Wood Stud
```

That's it.

No pilot holes.

No anchors.

No grommets.

## Screw spacing

I'd install:

- Across the top:
  - every **16–24 inches**
- Down each side:
  - every **24–30 inches**

The tarp weighs very little, so you don't need a screw at every stud unless you find the tarp billows more than you'd like.

## Shopping List

- ✅ **#10 × 1-1/4" exterior construction screws**

You're thinking of a different class of hardware, and I think it's actually a better fit.

If you're not trying to preserve the conduit as electrical conduit, there's no reason to flatten it.

I believe you're referring to **through-bolting** the joint:

```text
Front View

========================
        ○
        │
        │
        │
```

A hole is drilled completely through the horizontal EMT and completely through the vertical EMT where they intersect.

A machine bolt passes through both tubes.

The bolt is secured with:
- flat washer
- lock washer (or nylon lock nut)
- hex nut

The bolt acts as a **pin** connecting the two members.

### Advantages

- No special fittings.
- Very inexpensive.
- Much stronger than conduit straps.
- Easy to disassemble.
- Doesn't rely on friction.
- Uses hardware Home Depot stocks.

For your application, I'd probably use:

- **1/4"-20 or 5/16"-18 hex bolt**
- Length about **2½–3 inches**, depending on the outside diameter of the EMT and whether you add washers.
- Nylon lock nut so vibration won't loosen it.

The only thing I'd recommend is drilling the hole accurately so the members stay square.

In fact, if you use through-bolts, I would eliminate the conduit straps at the conduit-to-conduit joints entirely.

The revised design becomes:

- **Horizontal EMT → wall:** EMT straps into the wall studs.
- **Horizontal EMT → vertical EMT:** One through-bolt.
- **Vertical EMT → foot:** One through-bolt.

That leaves the only EMT straps in the entire project being the ones that fasten the horizontal conduit to the wall.

I think that's a cleaner, stronger, and simpler design than my earlier strap-based concept.

That geometry is much better than I had pictured.

If the slab is **24–30 inches long**, then when the **trailing edge on the infeed side** is still **12 inches from the blade**, the **leading edge has already extended 12–18 inches beyond the blade**. In other words, there is always a substantial length of slab on both sides of the blade during the cut.

That means you're not reaching past the blade to grab a small piece. Instead, you're transitioning from:
- **feeding** with the left hand on the infeed side,
- to **supporting or controlling** the already-cut portion on the outfeed side.

Mechanically, that's a much more stable situation than cutting individual 8–10 inch fillets, where your hands would have to approach the blade much more closely near the end of each cut.

The one thing I'd still pay attention to is avoiding pulling faster than you're feeding. A bandsaw blade is happiest when the work is being **fed into it** at a steady rate. If the outfeed hand starts doing most of the work, it can twist the slab slightly or encourage the blade to wander. Using the outfeed hand primarily to **keep the slab level and aligned** while the infeed hand provides the driving force generally gives the straightest cuts.

With a frozen slab that long, it also sounds like an **outfeed support** (a table, roller, or slick sheet) would be more valuable than a push stick. Once the slab extends well beyond the blade, supporting its weight reduces the tendency for the cut end to sag or rotate, making those three passes through the case even more repeatable.

That's a good precaution. Disconnecting the motor and sealing it in a plastic bag removes one of the biggest concerns when washing the saw.

There are still a few components I'd try to protect from direct high-pressure spray:

- **Blade guide bearings or guide blocks** – high pressure can flush out grease and force water into bearings.
- **Wheel bearings** – if your saw has sealed bearings they'll tolerate occasional moisture, but repeated pressure washing directly at them can shorten their life.
- **Switches and electrical connectors** – even with the motor removed, keep the switch and wiring as dry as practical.
- **Tension adjustment mechanism** – rinse it if needed, but avoid blasting directly into the threads.

Since you'll be cleaning after every use, I'd consider keeping a small maintenance kit at the station:

- Food-safe degreaser or detergent
- Nylon detail brushes
- Plastic scraper
- Wet/dry vacuum
- Steam cleaner
- Microfiber towels
- Compressed air or a small electric blower
- Food-grade lubricant for any parts the manufacturer specifies should be lubricated after cleaning

One thing I noticed from your setup is that the bandsaw is mounted to a plywood base. If you're going to be washing it frequently, you might eventually consider replacing that plywood with **HDPE (cutting-board material)** or another waterproof panel. Plywood tends to absorb moisture over time, making it harder to keep sanitary.

For your design, **I don't think you need tarp clips.**

Tarp clips are plastic clamps that grip the tarp and create a temporary attachment point where there isn't a factory grommet. They're useful when:
- you don't want to put holes in the tarp,
- you need an attachment between grommets,
- or you plan to take the tarp down frequently.

Since you're building a semi-permanent enclosure, drilling through the tarp is actually simpler.

### Wall attachment

```text
Wood stud
    │
Screw
    ▼
Large fender washer
════════════════════
      Tarp
════════════════════
Wood stud
```

Use:
- **#8 or #10 wood screws**
- **1-inch (or larger) fender washers**

The washer spreads the load over a much larger area than the screw head, making it much less likely that the tarp will tear.

### Don't screw directly through the tarp

If you drive the screw head directly into the tarp, eventually the plastic will tear around the head.

The fender washer acts like a built-in grommet.

### Spacing

I'd place screws approximately:
- every **16–24 inches** along the top,
- every **24–36 inches** down the sides.

You don't need many fasteners because the tarp weighs very little.

### For the EMT frame

I'd attach the tarp to the EMT differently.

Rather than drilling holes in the tarp there, I'd simply wrap it around the conduit and secure it with:

- zip ties,
- reusable Velcro straps,
- or short bungee cords through the factory grommets.

That way, if you ever change the frame or replace the tarp, you haven't created unnecessary holes.

So I'd revise today's shopping list by **removing the tarp clips** and instead adding:

- **1 package of 1-inch fender washers**
- **1 box of #8 or #10 wood screws**
- **1 bag of heavy-duty zip ties** (or reusable hook-and-loop straps) for attaching the tarp to the EMT.

I think that combination is cheaper, stronger, and better suited to the semi-permanent workstation you're building.

EMT (Electrical Metallic Tubing) is relatively thin-walled steel, so it's much easier to cut than black pipe or rigid conduit. Here are the common methods, ranked for your project.

| Tool | Cut Quality | Speed | Cost | Recommended |
|------|-------------|:-----:|:----:|:-----------:|
| Tubing cutter (EMT/conduit cutter) | ★★★★★ | Slow | $20–40 | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| Hacksaw | ★★★★☆ | Moderate | $10–20 | ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ |

### 1. Tubing cutter (my recommendation)

This looks like an oversized pipe cutter.

**Pros**
- Makes clean, square cuts.
- No sparks.
- No metal filings thrown everywhere.
- Easy to use indoors.

**Cons**
- Takes about a minute or two per cut.
- You'll usually need to ream or file the inside edge afterward.

For only 3–4 cuts, this is probably the nicest option.

---

### 2. Hacksaw

If you already own one, it's perfectly adequate.

Use:
- A **24 TPI** or **32 TPI** metal-cutting blade.

Clamp the EMT, make the cut, then deburr it with a file.

---

### 3. Angle grinder

Very fast, but:
- Throws sparks.
- Leaves a rougher edge.
- Requires eye protection, hearing protection, and gloves.

---

## Don't forget deburring

Whatever tool you use, the cut edge will be sharp.

Buy one of these:
- Conduit reamer
- Half-round file
- Flat mill file

Five seconds of deburring makes the conduit much safer to handle and easier to slide through straps or fittings.

For your application, I would **not** buy one of the large household steam mops. They excel at cleaning floors but are awkward for a bandsaw with lots of tight spaces.

Instead, I'd look for a **portable canister-style steam cleaner** with these capabilities:

### Boiler
- **Continuous boiler**, not a small trigger-operated steamer if your budget allows.
- At least **45–60 minutes** of continuous steaming before refilling.
- Fast heat-up (under 10 minutes).

### Steam pressure
- Approximately **50–75 psi**.
- Lower-pressure units struggle to force steam into the narrow blade guides and wheel housings.
- Much higher pressure isn't necessary and can just make more of a mess.

### Steam temperature
- Around **250–300°F (120–150°C)** at the nozzle.
- That's sufficient to soften fish proteins and fats while using relatively little water.

### Water tank
- At least **1 quart (1 liter)**.
- Larger is better if you're cleaning the workstation, tarps, and table in addition to the saw.

### Hose
This is surprisingly important.

I'd want:
- **6–8 ft hose minimum**
- Lightweight and flexible

You'll be walking around the saw rather than moving the cleaner constantly.

### Nozzle assortment

These are the attachments I'd actually use:

✔ Detail jet nozzle

- For blade guides
- Bearing housings
- Corners

✔ Nylon brushes

- Excellent for loosening fish residue while steaming

✔ Long lance

- Reach under the table
- Reach behind the wheels

✔ Flat brush with microfiber cover

- Stainless surfaces
- Tabletop
- Splash shields

### Continuous refill
If your budget allows, this is probably the single nicest feature.

Instead of waiting for the boiler to cool before refilling, you simply add water and continue cleaning.

### Wheels
I'd prefer a wheeled canister.

You have a fairly large workstation, and pulling a 10-pound cleaner around by its hose gets old quickly.

---

## How I'd use it

1. Remove large fish pieces.
2. Vacuum remaining chips/slush.
3. Steam the blade guides, wheel covers, table, and fence.
4. Brush while steaming.
5. Wipe away loosened residue.
6. Rinse if necessary.
7. Vacuum remaining water.
8. Allow to dry (or blow dry with compressed air).

---

## One feature I'd avoid

I wouldn't spend extra for a model that dispenses detergent. Fish residue comes off well with **steam and mechanical brushing**, and introducing detergent into the steam system just adds another thing to rinse and maintain.

## Budget

I'd expect to spend roughly:

- **$80–150:** Consumer handheld or small canister. Good if you're cleaning after occasional processing.
- **$150–300:** Mid-range canister with better pressure, longer runtime, and more accessories. This is the range I'd target for your operation.
- **$500+:** Commercial continuous-fill machines. Excellent, but probably hard to justify unless you're processing fish at a much larger scale.

Given everything you've described—processing entire cases in three passes, wanting to sanitize the saw after each session, and enclosing the workstation—a **mid-range canister steam cleaner with continuous steam, a long hose, and several detail brushes** would likely provide the best balance of performance, convenience, and cost.

Between those two, **canola oil was the better choice** for a food-contact machine. WD-40 is not intended as a food-contact lubricant.

However, canola oil has one major drawback: **it oxidizes and polymerizes** over time. The thin film eventually becomes sticky or varnish-like, especially where it's exposed to air. That sticky residue can actually trap fish proteins and make the saw harder to clean.

For a bandsaw used in food processing, I'd look for an **NSF H1 food-grade lubricant**. H1 lubricants are formulated for equipment where incidental food contact can occur.

Based on your description:

- One case contains **2 slabs**.
- Each slab contains **4 layers** of frozen fish.
- The two slabs stacked together are **just under the saw's 9-inch cutting height**.
- You only make **longitudinal (long-axis) cuts**.
- Therefore, **one cut slices through all 8 layers simultaneously**.
- If each fish needs to be divided into **3 long strips**, the entire case can be processed in **3 passes through the saw**.

That's a huge reduction in labor compared with cutting each fish individually.

The biggest advantages I see are:

- **Consistency:** Every strip is the same width because the fence controls the cut.
- **Speed:** Three controlled passes replace dozens of knife cuts.
- **Less operator fatigue:** You're guiding a frozen block rather than repeatedly sawing with a knife.
- **Better yield:** Straight cuts reduce variability and make portioning more predictable.

Since this bandsaw has become a critical piece of equipment, I'd start thinking of it like a production machine rather than just a tool. That means having:
- A spare blade on hand.
- A routine cleaning and lubrication schedule.
- Spare consumables (blade guides if they wear, drive belt if applicable).
- A log of when the blade was changed or sharpened, so you can replace it before cut quality declines.

One idea that might further improve your process is adding a **sliding carriage or pusher** that rides against the fence. Instead of pushing directly on the frozen fish, you'd place the slab in a tray or against a backstop and push the carriage. That can make each of the three passes smoother, improve consistency, and keep your hands farther from the blade while maintaining good control.

Given your current workflow, the bandsaw appears to have shifted from being a convenience to being the **bottleneck-eliminating step** in your fish preparation process. Keeping it reliable and easy to clean is likely to have a larger impact on your operation than almost any other equipment upgrade.

For your application (cutting frozen fish), I'd prioritize tools differently than for a woodworking shop. Fish residue is **protein and fat**, which becomes sticky and can harbor bacteria if it dries. The goal is to remove it before it dries rather than rely on brute force afterward.

Here's how I'd rank the tools:

### 1. Wet/dry shop vacuum ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
This would be one of my first purchases.

Benefits:
- Vacuum standing rinse water from the table and floor tarp.
- Remove slush, scales, and fish fragments.
- Leave the floor nearly dry so flies aren't attracted to moisture.
- Prevent puddles under the table.

A 6–9 gallon model is probably sufficient for this station.

### 2. Pressure washer ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆
Very useful, but I'd use it thoughtfully.

Pros:
- Excellent for the floor tarp.
- Cleans the table.
- Flushes the bandsaw frame.

Cons:
- A high-pressure jet can drive fish residue **deeper into bearings, electrical components, and tight crevices**.
- It can also aerosolize contaminants, so it's best used after gross debris has been removed and with electrical components protected.

I'd use a moderate-pressure, wide fan spray rather than a pinpoint nozzle on the saw itself.

### 3. Steam cleaner ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
For this application, I actually think this is more valuable than a pressure washer for the saw.

Steam:
- Softens dried protein.
- Melts fish fats.
- Penetrates small crevices.
- Uses very little water.
- Helps sanitize surfaces after cleaning.

A handheld steam cleaner with detail nozzles would be excellent for guides, blade guards, and other tight areas.

### 4. Air compressor ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆
Very helpful.

Use compressed air to:
- Blow water out of tight spaces after washing.
- Dry guide bearings and crevices.
- Reduce the time moisture sits on metal parts.

Just be aware it can also blow debris around, so use it after washing.

### 5. Nylon detailing brushes ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Buy several sizes.

- Toothbrush-sized
- Bottle brushes
- Long, narrow brushes for blade guides
- Larger scrub brushes

These are inexpensive and often do more work than power tools.

### 6. Squeegee ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
A simple floor squeegee lets you push rinse water toward the shop vac quickly. It's inexpensive and speeds cleanup.

### 7. Pump sprayer ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆
A 1–2 gallon pump sprayer is useful for:
- Applying detergent.
- Applying sanitizer after cleaning.
- Rinsing specific areas without using the pressure washer.

## One tool I would add that many people overlook

A **headlamp**.

Being able to shine light directly into the blade guides, lower wheel housing, and under the table makes it much easier to verify that no fish residue remains.

## My recommended cleaning workflow

1. Brush or scrape off large fish pieces.
2. Rinse with a pump sprayer or gentle hose.
3. Use nylon brushes on tight areas.
4. Steam-clean crevices and guides.
5. Vacuum water with the wet/dry vac.
6. Blow remaining moisture from inaccessible areas with compressed air (or allow to air dry if you don't have a compressor).
7. Lubricate any components that require lubrication according to the saw's manual, since repeated washing can remove protective films.

For a fish-processing workstation that will be cleaned frequently, I think the **best combination** is:

- **Wet/dry shop vac** (essential)
- **Handheld steam cleaner** (excellent for the saw)
- **Pressure washer** (best for the floor tarp, walls, and surrounding work area rather than close-range cleaning of the saw)
- **Detail brushes and a floor squeegee** (low cost, high value)

That combination will generally clean more thoroughly and with less risk to the saw than relying on a pressure washer alone.

The concern isn't that your hand is close to the blade while cutting—it's that **reaching to the outfeed side of a running bandsaw to pull stock through creates an opportunity for your hand to drift back toward the blade or for the slab to shift unexpectedly.** With frozen fish, the surface can also be slippery.

A safer technique is to let the **left hand continue feeding from the infeed side** while the right hand on the outfeed side does little more than **support or guide** the slab after it has fully cleared the blade, rather than actively pulling it through.

Since your slab is 24–30 inches long, another option is to make the machine do the work by improving the outfeed support:

- Add an outfeed table or roller so the slab stays level after it passes the blade.
- Keep the fence long enough that the slab remains guided throughout the cut.
- Use a simple pusher only for the **last few inches** if the trailing edge ever gets too close to the blade—not because the whole cut requires it.

Given your workflow, I don't think a traditional woodworking push stick is the right tool anyway. If you ever decide you want one, a **wide HDPE or UHMW pusher block** that contacts the full back edge of the frozen slab would be much more stable than a narrow stick.

The fact that you're cutting the entire case in only three passes also means there are **very few blade interactions per case**, which reduces repetitive handling compared with cutting individual fillets. I'd focus on keeping those three passes as stable and repeatable as possible rather than trying to speed them up further. The biggest gains now are likely to come from good support surfaces and consistent feeding rather than increasing feed rate.

- Wall vertical: **8 ft (96")**
- Freestanding vertical: **8 ft (96")**
- Crossbar: **40"**
- Foot: **32"** (I think 30–36" is the sweet spot)

Total required:

- 96 + 96 + 40 + 32 = **264 inches**

Two 10-ft sticks provide only **240 inches**.

So **two sticks are not enough** if you want both an 8-foot upright and a 32-inch foot.

## If you absolutely want to use only two sticks

You have to reduce the height.

For example:

| Piece | Length |
|--------|-------:|
| Wall upright | 84" (7 ft) |
| Freestanding upright | 84" (7 ft) |
| Crossbar | 40" |
| Foot | 32" |
| **Total** | **240"** |

**Stick 1 (120")**
- 84" upright
- 36" remaining

**Stick 2 (120")**
- 84" upright
- 36" remaining

Now use the two 36" remnants:
- One becomes the **36" foot**
- Cut the other into a **36" crossbar**, or if you want a 40" crossbar, shorten the foot to **32"** and cut:
  - 40" crossbar

- 24" scrap

**Stick 2**
- 96" upright
- 24" scrap

- 40" crossbar

That changes the design considerably. Since you're cutting **frozen, packaged fish** rather than wood, your enclosure is less about dust collection and more about:

1. **Keeping flies away from exposed product.**
2. **Reducing wind that can carry insects in.**
3. **Creating a clean work area that can be sanitized.**
4. **Keeping the operator comfortable.**

The fan is then functioning as an **air curtain**, not a dust exhaust.

## I would orient the enclosure like this

```
          Existing wall
 ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │                              │
 │  Bandsaw          Fan --->   │
 │                              │
 │                              │
 └──────────────────────────────┘
 Existing wall          New tarp wall

==============================   <- open operator side
      You stand here
```

The fan should blow **toward the open side**, creating a continuous airflow out of the enclosure. Flies generally avoid flying into a steady stream of moving air, so this helps keep them away from the fish.

## Floor tarp

A floor tarp makes even more sense here than it would for woodworking because:

- Meltwater can be contained.
- Packaging debris is easier to clean up.
- Fish particles don't end up on the garage floor.
- At the end of the day you can wash and sanitize the tarp.

I'd use a **heavy-duty waterproof tarp** rather than a thin disposable one.

## Right-side support

Since that side lacks a wall, I'd make it sturdy enough to support not only the tarp but also clips or hooks for tools. For example:

- Two 2×4 uprights about 7–8 ft tall.
- One top crossmember.
- Optional lower crossmember about knee height to stiffen the frame.
- Weights or sandbags on the feet so it can't tip if the fan catches the tarp.

## Food safety consideration

One thing I noticed is the **bandsaw is mounted on plywood**. Since you'll be processing packaged frozen fish, that's less of a contamination concern than if you were cutting unpackaged food. If you ever transition to cutting unwrapped fish on that setup, I'd recommend replacing or covering the plywood with a smooth, non-absorbent material (such as HDPE sheet or stainless steel) because plywood is difficult to sanitize thoroughly after repeated exposure to moisture.

Overall, I think the three-sided enclosure plus the fan blowing outward through the open front is a practical approach for reducing flies while maintaining easy access to the workstation.

- Extremely rigid.

After thinking about your construction method, I'd actually recommend **two-hole straps**, not one-hole straps.

The one-hole straps are intended to hold conduit **against a flat surface**. They don't do as good a job when you're trying to join one conduit to another because they can pivot around the single fastener.

With your concept, a two-hole strap has several advantages:

- **Less twisting.** Two screws keep the strap from rotating.
- **Larger contact area.** The conduit is held more evenly.
- **Higher rigidity.** The joint behaves more like a clamp than a hinge.
- **Better load distribution.** If the tarp catches wind, the force is shared by two screws instead of one.

Your joint would look like this:

```
      Horizontal EMT
========================

      [=====]
        ||
        ||
     Vertical EMT
        ||
```

The two-hole strap wraps around the horizontal conduit, and the two screws go into the vertical conduit.

### I'd actually use two straps per joint

One on the front:

```
   [=====]
```

and one on the back:

```
   [=====]
========================
   [=====]
```

That effectively clamps the horizontal conduit between two straps and makes the connection much stiffer. Since EMT is inexpensive to drill, this is an easy way to improve rigidity without specialized fittings.

The only place I'd still use one-hole straps is where you're fastening the **rear upright to the existing wall**, because that's exactly what they're designed for. There, the conduit is against a flat surface, and the strap simply holds it in place. Everywhere you're **joining conduit to conduit**, I'd choose two-hole straps.

If the chuck is completely closed around the bit and **won't open at all**, the jaws are likely jammed. Try the following, in order:

1. **Remove the bit tension.**
   - Push the Phillips bit *slightly inward* while turning the chuck key to open it. Sometimes the bit wedges the jaws.

2. **Lubricate the jaws.**
   - Put a few drops of penetrating oil into the front of the chuck where the three jaws meet the bit.
   - Wait 15–30 minutes.

3. **Shock the mechanism.**
   - Insert the chuck key.
   - While applying opening force to the key, lightly tap the end of the key handle with a small hammer. A few light taps are better than one hard hit.

4. **Clamp the drill body.**
   - If you have a vise, clamp the drill body (not the chuck) with padding.
   - Apply steady pressure to the chuck key while gently tapping it.

If it still won't open, there may be a broken internal jaw or scroll mechanism.

From your photo, it looks like you have a **keyed drill chuck**. If it won't open, it's usually one of three things: it's overtightened, it's rusted/gummed up, or the jaws are jammed.

Try these in order:

1. **Make sure you're turning the correct direction.**
   - Insert the chuck key into one of the gear holes.
   - To **open** the chuck (spread the jaws), rotate the key **counterclockwise when viewed from the front of the chuck** (looking at the bit). If you're holding the drill in a different orientation, it can be easy to get turned around.

2. **Use all three key holes.**
   - If it won't budge from one position, move the key to another gear hole and try again. This applies force more evenly and can free a jam.

3. **Apply penetrating oil.**
   - Put a few drops of penetrating oil (PB Blaster, Liquid Wrench, or even WD-40 if that's all you have) where the three jaws meet.
   - Let it sit for 10–30 minutes, then work the chuck back and forth.

4. **Tap the key lightly.**
   - With the key engaged, give the handle of the chuck key a few light taps with a small hammer. Don't hit hard—just enough to shock the mechanism loose.

5. **Grip the chuck body if needed.**
   - Hold the drill firmly, or clamp the drill body (not the chuck) in a padded vise while turning the key.

This is not a forensic inquiry. I'm just curious
How much video should a 32GB body cam record in hours/minutes

That makes sense. For a 32 GB body camera like yours, it's interesting how much footage fits because the compression is fairly efficient.

A good rule of thumb is:

- **Highest quality (1296p):** about **4–5 hours**
- **1080p:** about **5–6 hours**
- **720p:** about **8–10 hours**
- **480p:** about **12–16 hours**

For comparison, a typical police officer working an **8–10 hour shift** would generally need:
- **64 GB** if recording most of the shift in 1080p, or
- A camera configured to overwrite the oldest footage once storage fills.

Most body cameras don't record continuously all day. They're usually activated only during calls, traffic stops, or other incidents. That means **32 GB is often enough for an entire shift** in typical use, even though it wouldn't hold 8–10 hours of uninterrupted high-definition video.

A standard keyed chuck **does not** open by threading the gear ring away from the chuck body. The **gear ring**, **chuck sleeve**, and **chuck body** should normally remain assembled as a unit while the internal scroll moves the jaws.

If, when you keep turning the chuck, the **gear ring appears to walk away from the sleeve/body**, there are a few likely possibilities.

### Possibility 1 (most likely): The internal scroll has become disengaged from the jaws.
The sleeve and gear ring are still turning, but the scroll is no longer driving the jaws. Since the jaws don't move, continued turning can make part of the chuck assembly shift axially, giving the appearance that the gear ring is unscrewing.

### Possibility 2: The retaining mechanism has failed.
Many keyed chucks have a retaining ring, snap ring, or swaged lip that prevents the gear ring/sleeve from moving off the body. If that retainer has broken or come loose, the gear ring can creep upward while you continue rotating it.

### Possibility 3: The chuck has partially come apart.
Heavy force—especially using a wrench and the drill motor instead of a chuck key—can occasionally cause the chuck to partially disassemble. Once that happens, the outer sleeve may continue rotating without transmitting motion to the jaw mechanism.

## I'd like to verify exactly what is moving.

As you continue turning:

- **Does the entire upper section** (the conical nose with the keyhole) move upward away from the lower cylindrical sleeve?
- Or **only the toothed gear ring** moves upward?
- Or does the gap open **between the gear ring and the lower sleeve**?

Even better, if you can take **another photo after you've turned it until it separates as far as it will go**, I can usually identify exactly which component is moving and tell you whether the chuck can be repaired or should simply be replaced.

That explains why your chuck is in the condition shown. Those methods will make the chuck work in the absence of a key, but they also put loads on parts that weren't designed for them.

Here's what each method is doing:

1. **Holding the chuck sleeve with a wrench while pulsing the drill**
   - The motor supplies the torque.
   - The wrench prevents the sleeve from rotating.
   - The torque is transmitted through the chuck's internal scroll mechanism.
   - This produces much higher shock loads than turning it with a chuck key, especially if you "bump" the trigger.

2. **Using an Allen wrench or screwdriver in the keyhole**
   - This is closer to how the chuck was intended to operate.
   - However, the keyhole is meant to accept a chuck key whose gear meshes with the **chuck gear ring**.
   - A plain screwdriver or Allen wrench pushes on only one side of the hole, so it can burr or egg-shape the hole if a lot of force is required.

From your earlier photo I also notice:
- The **gear ring teeth** appear somewhat rounded from use.
- The chuck has surface rust and grime.
- The bit looks heavily worn.
- The chuck body doesn't appear cracked.

### Before we discuss fixing it, I'd like to establish one more piece of terminology.

Internally, the chuck contains:
- **Three jaws** (the parts that grip the bit)
- **Scroll (jaw screw)** – a spiral-threaded ring that moves all three jaws together.
- **Jaw guides** – slots the jaws slide in.

Those internal parts are often the source of problems.

### My first question

When you say the chuck "won't open," which of these best describes it?

**A.** The chuck sleeve turns normally, but the jaws don't move.

**B.** The chuck sleeve is extremely hard to turn.

**C.** The sleeve and gear ring rotate together as one solid piece, but the jaws stay closed.

**D.** The sleeve moves a tiny amount (perhaps 1/16 of a turn) and then stops.

**E.** Something else.

Also, is the drill **forward/reverse reversible**, and is it **corded or cordless**? That affects a couple of troubleshooting options.
The chuck sleeve turns and the jaws wont open. Continously turning the chuck key seems to cause the gear ring to separate from it as if they might be threaded

I don't have a key for the chuck. I've been opening and closing the jaws by either holding the chuck sleeve with a wrench and running motor to open/close them or by inserting an Allen wrench or screwdriver into the keyhole and in combination with a wrench at the chuck sleeve opening and closing.

I want to discuss a problem with this set of parts on a drill. Create a labeled version of this photo where the name of each component is clearly indicated so that we can have a common reference and vocabulary
The gap appears between the lower sleeve and gear ring. If I'm holding the sleeve with a wrench and engage the motor should the gear ring rotate or remain stationary?

Under normal operation, **the gear ring should rotate with the chuck sleeve**. They are effectively one assembly.

If you hold the **lower chuck sleeve** firmly with a wrench and engage the motor:

- **The chuck sleeve should remain stationary** (because you're holding it).
- **The gear ring should also remain stationary** relative to the sleeve.
- There should be **no visible gap opening** between the sleeve and the gear ring.

If, instead, the **gear ring rotates or climbs upward while the sleeve stays put**, that's a strong indication something inside the chuck has failed or partially come apart. The gear ring is no longer being retained correctly.

### One simple test

With the drill **unplugged or the battery removed**:

1. Grip the **lower sleeve** with one hand.
2. Grip the **gear ring** (the toothed ring) with the other.
3. Try to move them **axially** (pull them apart and push them together).
4. Then try to rotate the gear ring relative to the sleeve.

Tell me:
- Can you **pull the gear ring away** from the sleeve by hand?
- Can you rotate the **gear ring independently** of the sleeve, or do they always rotate together?

Those two observations will tell us whether the failure is in the chuck's retaining mechanism or deeper in the jaw/scroll mechanism.

Fair point. If the only issue is whether the **native aluminum oxide layer** is stable enough to act as the contact surface, then the answer is: **not for the kind of mechanical grinding you're describing.**

The reason isn't that aluminum oxide is unstable—it is quite stable under many ordinary conditions. The limitation is that:

- The oxide film is **extremely thin** (on the order of nanometers).
- It is bonded to **very soft aluminum** underneath.
- As soon as you apply the pressure and shear needed to pulverize a clump, the foil plastically deforms. The oxide cracks and reforms while the underlying aluminum is exposed and deformed.

So during grinding, your contact surface is effectively not "aluminum oxide"; it's a continuously deforming aluminum substrate with a regenerating oxide film. That means there is a real possibility of transferring microscopic aluminum particles into the material being ground.

If your goal is simply to break up a dry clump and a trace amount of aluminum contamination is unimportant, a piece of household foil can work in an emergency. If you need the resulting powder to remain free of metal contamination, the oxide layer on foil is not thick or robust enough to rely on as a protective grinding surface.

That's a real effect, and it comes from the geometry of the mesh rather than any special chemical property of stainless steel.

When you press a clump against woven stainless mesh:

- **The wire intersections act as many tiny crushing points.** Instead of one large contact area, the force is concentrated at dozens or hundreds of small contacts, which helps fracture brittle agglomerates.
- **The openings provide a built-in size limit.** Once fragments become small enough to pass through an aperture, they tend to fall through and are no longer subjected to further grinding. In that sense, the mesh acts as both a grinder and a coarse classifier.
- **Material that remains above the mesh** continues to experience repeated crushing until it is either reduced enough to pass or is too tough to fracture further.

The resulting particle-size distribution is not identical to the mesh opening because particle shape and orientation matter. For example, elongated or flaky particles may pass through openings smaller than one of their dimensions, while irregular particles may require being considerably smaller before they can pass. So the mesh provides a **practical upper bound** on particle size rather than a precise cutoff.

Stainless steel mesh is also much harder and more wear-resistant than household aluminum foil, so it maintains its geometry under pressure much better and is less likely to deform during this kind of mechanical comminution. That makes it a much more effective improvised grinding and screening surface for suitable dry, brittle materials.

For regular household aluminum foil, is the thin coating of aluminum oxide on its surface sufficiently stable that i could use a piece of foil in a pinch to create a fine powder from some a clump of material that would be amenable to pulverization by mortar and pestle

I have used stainless mesh to grind and it works surprisingly well with the added benefit that one can determine a measure of particle size if the material is able to pass through the mesh while grinding

The aluminum-oxide film on household foil is chemically stable for many dry, neutral materials, but **the foil itself is a poor surface for pulverizing**.

The oxide layer is only a few nanometers thick. It will not function as a durable ceramic coating: pressure and scraping from a mortar, pestle, spoon, or other tool will crease, tear, and abrade the underlying soft aluminum. That can introduce tiny aluminum or foil fragments into the powder.

In a pinch, foil is acceptable only for **lightly crushing a dry, nonreactive material**, such as folding it around a brittle clump and pressing gently. Avoid it when:

- The powder will be eaten, inhaled, smoked, used medically, or subjected to chemical analysis.
- The substance is acidic, alkaline, salty and damp, or otherwise reactive with aluminum.
- You need to grind forcefully or achieve a very fine, uncontaminated powder.

A clean glass, glazed ceramic, stainless-steel surface, or even a heavy polyethylene bag placed on a hard surface is usually better. For mortar-and-pestle grinding, put the material directly in the mortar rather than lining it with foil.
